beats.text: One click sent nine hundred million dollars to the wrong people.
Three people approved it and nobody stopped it.
It was supposed to be eight million and this is what left the bank.
It was gone before anyone looked up.
But nobody hacked the bank.
And nobody stole a thing.
And here is the wildest part because the bank never got it back.
A judge refused and called it one of the biggest blunders in banking history.
So who clicked and who kept the money and why did the law let them?
This is the nine hundred million dollar click.
Imagine you work at a bank.
Your screen shows three small boxes. You tick one.
Then you go home.
And by morning your employer is missing nine hundred million dollars.
It starts with a makeup company.
In two thousand sixteen Revlon borrowed almost two billion dollars.
The money came from hundreds of lenders.
And Citibank sat in the middle.
Its job was boring.
Revlon pays the bank. The bank pays the lenders.
Citibank never risks a cent of its own money.
Until August the eleventh.
That day Revlon owed a small interest payment.
Seven point eight million dollars.
The payment was built in a banking program called Flexcube.
And at Citibank a big payment needs three people.
One builds it. One checks it. One approves it.
They call it the six eyes rule.
But Flexcube was old and strange.
To send a small payment it first pretended to pay off the whole loan.
Then it parked the big part in an inside account that goes nowhere.
So the money never really leaves. If you tick the right boxes.
And that was the trap.
Sending only the interest meant ticking three boxes.
They ticked one.
A contractor in India built the payment.
His colleague checked it.
And a senior manager in Delaware approved it.
So who clicked? All three of them did.
At five forty five the vault opened.
Not seven point eight million. Almost nine hundred million.
Every dollar of the loan plus the interest.
And it was not Revlon's money. It was Citibank's own.
Then everyone went home.
And the mistake sat there all night.
The next morning a manager ran a routine check.
The numbers did not match.
Almost nine hundred million dollars was missing.
This is what should have gone out.
And this is what did.
So Citibank did the only thing it could.
It asked for the money back.
And most lenders said sure.
About three hundred eighty five million dollars came home.
Now remember Revlon.
That year its stores were shut by the pandemic.
So for a lender getting every dollar back early felt like a miracle.
And miracles are hard to give back.
But ten investment firms looked at the money.
And they said no.
Together they were holding half a billion dollars.
Inside those firms the group chats lit up.
Traders typed words like unbelievable and accidental and overpayment.
So they knew something was off.
But here is the part that made this case famous.
Revlon really did owe them that money.
Every dollar. To the cent.
The loan just was not due for three more years.
Now put yourself in their chair.
Half a billion dollars just landed in your account.
It is money you were owed anyway.
Would you send it back?
So it was not a robbery.
And it was not a trick.
It was their own loan paid back early by accident.
And New York has an old rule for exactly this.
It comes from a case in nineteen ninety one.
If someone pays off a real debt by mistake you can keep the money.
But only if you did not know it was a mistake.
So the whole trial came down to one question.
Did the lenders know?
Citibank said of course they knew because nobody repays a loan three years early.
The lenders said a bank that size does not make a mistake that big.
In February two thousand twenty one the judge picked a side.
The lenders could keep all of it.
Half a billion dollars. Gone for good.
And the judge did not spare the bank.
Then it got worse because the regulators arrived.
That fine covered years of problems and not just one click.
But Citibank was not done.
It appealed.
And for nineteen months half a billion dollars sat frozen.
Then in September two thousand twenty two three new judges read the same facts.
And they saw the opposite.
The loan was not due for three years. So nobody was owed that money yet.
And a careful investor would have picked up the phone.
One call. Is this a mistake?
Nobody made that call.
So the ten firms had to send it all back.
By December the case was closed.
Think about that for a second.
Six eyes looked at one screen.
And the most expensive mistake in banking walked right past them.
Because each of them thought someone else had checked.
So Citibank got its money back.
It only took two years and two courts.
And a place in history it never wanted.
All of it because of three little boxes.
And one click that nobody questioned.
And here is the part that matters for you.
If a bank ever drops money into your account by mistake it is not yours.
Even nine hundred million dollars had to go back.
So before you click anything check the boxes.
